instruction.what: Step 3.1, the elements of one subgroup (stage 4, C1; the end of the loop for the subgroup): what the evidence of the subgroup shows of the elements of a behaviour of the inner being. The input is the evidence observations of the subgroup by marker (`to_take_up`, the senses first, then the 2.1 findings and the older evidence), not the verses; the verses are kept for an occasional read-back. A finding is a building block, never a claim about the behaviour as a whole (that is stage 5).
read: Read the observations to take up, in order: the senses (1.1) and their enrichments (1.2) first, then the 2.1 findings (pairings, qualifiers, entities, direction, double meanings), then the older evidence. The inner-being workings work more with the senses than with the surfaces, so findings rest on the senses first.

For each item a finding may use (`uses`): what is done and its mode (operation, with its chain), whether a refusal or a pursuit (polarity), what it is directed at (object), the outward act (enactment), the other party with the route (party), the circumstance, and what a qualifier or a variation of the word gives the working (role, the dimension). Never the meaning of the word (stage 1).

Read the older inner-being observations (`older_inner_being`) with them: each is considered first, accepted with a trace to evidence, restated where it says more than the evidence, consumed where a finding says the same, merged, or deleted where it cannot be made true.
Go back to a verse (`verses`) only where the evidence does not settle the question, and say why.
write: Fill `answer.findings`: each one observation, with a `key` unique in the answer, `kind` (of the item's kinds), `text`, `basis` (stated or read), `parts` with `item` (one of `uses`) and what the item needs (with `grounds`), and `nodes`: a `traced` node on each observation it rests on (from `to_take_up` or `may_rest_on_besides`) and an `occurrence` node, with its `role` chosen from the verse (characteristic, qualifier, object, relational target, enactment or standalone), on the occurrences those observations cover.
An occurrence outside the observations a finding rests on is allowed only with a `read_back` entry on the finding: {verse: the osis id, why}.
`not_used`: {observation id: reason} for every observation to take up that no finding rests on. Every one is rested on or declared, never both.

`older`: answer, once, each older inner-being observation (`older_inner_being`) that has a node on an occurrence your findings name (RW-13; the record lists any it misses, and refuses an answer to one on no named occurrence: those are shown, not demanded, IB-05): keep (with nature inner_being: it stands, traced to evidence), restate, merge, consume (carriers ["this"] or ids, mapping), delete_neither, or defer (collection, nature, finding).
`existing`: answer every earlier reading (`earlier_readings`: inner being of an earlier grouping on these occurrences) with accept, modify, delete, merge or leave, and its reason.
The text says what the evidence shows of the element; it names its verses; it never restates a verse and never states the behaviour as a whole.
Then: Collection-Build.ps1 -Action RecordElements -File <the answer file> (-Check to preview). The record refuses the whole file on any fault and lists every fault.

keep.text: Stage 4 starts from the observations, not the verses (researcher, #2526 Q7, 2026-11-21): the subgroups and the stage 3 observations on them are the input, the behaviours are discovered from analysing them, and the base data is read back into only occasionally. Every finding of step 3.1 or 3.2 rests on named observations (a traced node on each, with an occurrence node as well) and its occurrence nodes lie within the occurrences those observations cover; an occurrence outside them is allowed only where the finding records a read-back (the verse and why). Each node has a role from reading.node_roles other than lexical, chosen by the reading. A 3.3 finding carries nodes on the occurrences of both sides in the shared verses.

A finding of a stage 4 row is checked by the rules of observationrecord.check and check_item_parts (kind, text, basis, route, parts.item and what the item needs, node roles, collection of each node) and by RG, RW and RS, which are not restated here: one observation for each finding, never a duplicate, with a node on each word it applies to (RO11, RW-03); founded in the observations and never a restatement of the verse (B:131); parts.item is one of the items the row's item uses (cfg_setting layer.reading). An observation whose nodes all bear on an act is refused: those words are nodes of the observation of the act. A finding is a building block of a behaviour and never a claim (stage 5).

Nothing the step reads is lost on the way to stage 5. Step 3.1: every stage 3 observation of the subgroup is rested on by a finding or declared in not_used with its reason in words. Step 3.2: every 3.1 observation of the collection is gathered into a behaviour (a traced node on it from a flag finding of type discovery) or declared in not_gathered with its reason, and the row has at least one behaviour unless it is recorded as none with its reason. A behaviour names and gathers; it makes no claim about what the behaviour is.

An earlier inner-being observation with a node on the occurrences of a 3.1 row (any stage but lexical, layer-1, layer-2 and layer-3) is shown in the pull for information and may be actioned in `existing`: accepted, modified, deleted, merged or left, each with its reason, through observationrecord (RW-01, RW-09); nothing is demanded of it, and it counts for nothing in the check. A row answered again withdraws its earlier observations with the reason. Every older live observation with a node on an occurrence of the row is answered in fill.older at the record of the row (RW-13); this rule's `existing` actions of stage 4 are unchanged.

Every live observation marked inner_being holds at least one live traced node on a live observation marked evidence, unless it is recorded self-evidencing: it quotes its verse in full and holds a word node for every word it relies on. A traced node never points at a deleted observation. A trace points first at existing evidence; an evidence observation is created only when none states the fact and it states what the nodes and the quotation do not. An inner-being observation traced to evidence not yet marked is pending, not failed.

Find the main inner-being operation, and give every word that bears on it its role in this finding (cfg_setting reading.node_roles): characteristic, qualifier and what it gives the characteristic, object or content, relational target, or enactment. A word read in the verse that holds nothing for the inner being is standalone. The role comes from this verse, never from the cluster tag. Where a standalone word proves to qualify a characteristic, it is a qualifier of it.

A qualifier gets no separate account of itself, but what it gives the characteristic it binds to is evaluated for its value and recorded as a qualification finding, applied by its nodes to the qualifier (role qualifier) and the characteristic (role characteristic). What it gives can vary widely: grade, nature, impact, size, relation, a measure, strengthening, ground, cause, object, setting or bait are examples, not a list (#2273 D9). A qualifier whose usage varies across contexts may earn its own reading later.

Record the parties: who bears the act, who causes it, who is acted on (source, target, impact, purpose), and the route (cfg_enum observation_route). A non-human being is never itself a HIB; a collective stays one HIB; an implied party is named as referential, never asserted.
Never close a verse or item on 'not X'. A role label is never a verdict; the close records what the verse is. Silence about the inner being is a finding, recorded as data with its reason.
A phenomenon hidden behind a stated or refrained act may be named, with the verb, clause or stated silence that grounds it, and whether it is stated or read.
Keep the source of an interior state apart from the source of an enablement to act.

A tagged word that works adverbially in an occurrence (a noun with a preposition qualifying the predicate, as 'in the counsel of the wicked') is a qualifier there, not the verse's characteristic. The role is per occurrence: the same word may be the characteristic elsewhere.
In a simile, the predicates of the vehicle (the tree that yields, does not wither) are read for what they say of the one compared (the tenor), not as the vehicle's own acts.
One observation per finding, never a duplicate description; a finding applying to several verses or words carries several nodes, each with the word's role in it.
One observation per finding: the same description is never written twice. Applied to another verse, word or scope it gains a node on the existing observation.
Observation text is concise and tied to this verse's content, never a restatement of the word's dictionary sense. A transliteration is never given without its gloss.

An observation is created with its marker (ib_observation.nature, from the item answered, cfg_setting layer.reading items.<item>.nature; a finding file never sets it) and every word node with the columns of layer.reading node_required. A column the data cannot give (layer.reading node_gap_columns: an empty morph in the source row, a surface with no placement in the collection index) is left empty and its reason is kept on the node (disposition_note); any other missing column refuses the whole file and nothing is written. A trace to a deleted observation is refused (IB-07).

Evidence states what the data are or show, tied to a verse. Inner being states how something works in the inner being, based on evidence, a building block of the stage 5 claims. The marker (ib_observation.nature) follows the content and purpose of the observation, never its stage (RS-04): an observation of any stage may be inner being when it traces to evidence. One that states both is split. The marker is set when the observation is created, by the item that is answered (cfg_setting layer.reading items.<item>.nature); a finding file never sets it; the validation changes it only where the content shows the item's nature does not hold.

asks: What do the stage 3 observations of this subgroup (its definition, its Strong's enrichment, its pairings, qualifiers, entities, direction, relations and double meanings, with the stage 1 senses) show of the elements of a behaviour of the inner being: what is done and its mode, whether a refusal or a pursuit, what it is directed at, the outward act, the other party with the route, the circumstance, the chain of operations, and the dimensions of the working (what a qualifier or a variation of the word gives it, from the lexical variation the stage 3 observations record)? Each finding is one observation that rests on named observations (a traced node on each) and carries nodes on the occurrences those observations cover, with the role each has; an occurrence outside them is allowed only with a read-back (the verse and why). Every stage 3 observation of the subgroup is rested on by a finding or declared not used, with the reason. A finding is a building block and never a claim about the behaviour as a whole (stage 5).

uses.name: its role: the qualifier and what it gives the characteristic
whether the act is a refusal or a pursuit
what the act is directed at or against
the outward act the inner act produces, where the verse states one
the other party and the sequence, with the route
how it appears here: the circumstance of the verse
the operation as an action description (who or what does what), its mode, the primary one
the chain of operations the verse links in sequence
a typed flag: data-quality, or discovery for the claims process

to_take_up.text: Reasoning as argument put to other people: Paul reasons with Jews and others in the synagogue, the market and the hall of Tyrannus and before Felix, and the Lord invites the people to argue the case out together. The word is spoken argument with a hearer and a matter, aimed at persuading or setting right; the Greek verb is of discourse and the Hebrew verb of arguing a case. Verses: Act 17:2, Act 1

Reasoning inside the mind: the reckoning of a child in 1Cor 13:11, a way of working things out that is given up in adulthood, and the reasoning in the hearts of the disciples in Luk 9:47, which Jesus knows. Both are reasoning held within a person, not argued to another. Verses: Luk 9:47, 1Cor 13:11.

Reason as understanding, the sound mind: in Dan 4 the king's reason returns to him when he lifts his eyes to heaven, and with it his kingdom and splendor. The word names the faculty itself. Verses: Dan 4:34, Dan 4:36.

Reason as the ground or cause of something: the cause of a coming, the ground of a charge, 'for this reason' and 'by reason of' as links to what an act or a state rests on, and the reason an act was done or a person appeared. The words are nouns and linking phrases of cause, in many Hebrew and Greek words, and carry no act of thinking. Verses: Gen 41:31, Gen 47:13, Num 18:32, Jos 5:4, 1Sa 20:29, 1

Reason denied: 'for no reason' is the Hebrew adverb of without cause, said of fearing God for nothing and of contending with a man who has done no harm. It is the absence of a ground. Verses: Job 1:9, Pro 3:30.
Reason as readiness to be persuaded: the wisdom from above is 'open to reason', a trait of the person who yields to others. It is a character trait of the one reasoned with. Verses: Jam 3:17.

Reason as an account given: the believer is to be ready to give a reason to anyone who asks, an explanation of the hope that is in him. It is a spoken account in answer to a question. Verses: 1Pe 3:15.

The codes of this sense are G1256 (to dispute, 7), H3198 (to rebuke, 1). The Greek G1256 is the verb of discourse and argument and the Hebrew H3198 is of arguing a case, which agree with reasoning put to other people. The lexicon entry of the main code G1256 gives: to reason, discuss, discourse; to argue, dispute. Verses: Isa 1:18, Act 19:8, Act 24:25, Act 19:9, Act 17:17, Act 17:2, Act 18:4, Act

The codes of this sense are G1261 (reasoning, 1), G3049 (to count, 1). G3049 is the verb of reckoning and G1261 the noun of reasoning and thought, which agree with reasoning held within a person. The lexicon entry of the main code G1261 gives: thought, doubt; argument, dispute. Verses: Luk 9:47, 1Cor 13:11.

The codes of this sense are H4486 (knowledge, 2). H4486 is knowledge and the power of knowing, which agrees with reason as the sound mind. The lexicon entry of the main code H4486 gives: knowledge, power of knowing. Verses: Dan 4:36, Dan 4:34.

The codes of this sense are G1223 (through/because of, 4), G0156 (cause/charge, 4), G5124 (that, 3), H6440I (face: because, 2), H5921A (upon, 2), H1697M (word: because, 2), G5484 (because of, 2), H3651C (so, 1), H1961 (to be, 1), G2596 (according to, 1), G0302 (if, 1), G1352 (therefore, 1), G1519 (toward, 1). The codes are prepositions, conjunctions, adverbs and nouns of cause (G0156 cause, G1352

The codes of this sense are H2600 (for nothing, 2). H2600 is for nothing or without cause, which agrees with the denial of a ground. The lexicon entry of the main code H2600 gives: freely, for nothing, without cause. Verses: Job 1:9, Pro 3:30.

The codes of this sense are G2138 (compliant, 1). G2138 is easily persuaded and compliant, which agrees with readiness to be persuaded. The lexicon entry of the main code G2138 gives: submissive, obedient, compliant. Verses: Jam 3:17.

The codes of this sense are G3056 (word, 1). G3056 is a word or thing uttered, which agrees with an account given. The lexicon entry of the main code G3056 gives: word, spoken or written, often with a focus on the content of a communication (note the many contextual translations in NIV); matter, thing.. Verses: 1Pe 3:15.

The surface reason renders eighteen codes. As a word of the mind it is G3056 in 1Pe 3:15 (an account given) and H4486 in Dan 4:34 and Dan 4:36 (understanding restored), both nouns, and G2138 in Jam 3:17, an adjective (open to persuasion); as a verb it is H3198 in Isa 1:18 (to argue a case together). Elsewhere it is part of a phrase of cause: H6440I in Gen 41:31, H5921A, H1697M, H3651C, G1223, G512
The surface reasoned carries two codes: G1256 in Act 17:2, Act 17:17, Act 18:4, Act 18:19 and Act 24:25, where Paul discourses with others, and G3049 in 1Co 13:11, where a child reckons for himself.

The surface reasoning carries two codes: G1261 in Luk 9:47, the reasoning held within the hearts of the disciples, and G1256 in Act 19:8 and Act 19:9, where Paul argues with others in the synagogue and the hall of Tyrannus.

In Act 17:2, Act 17:17, Act 18:4 and Act 19:8 the verb of reasoning (G1256) is qualified by time and frequency: on three Sabbaths, every day, every Sabbath, for three months. In Act 18:19 there qualifies the leaving of the others, not the reasoning. The qualifiers tell when and how often Paul reasoned, not how.
In 1Cor 13:11 the verb reasoned (G3049) is qualified by a comparison, like a child (G3516), the same qualifier set on spoke and thought before it; the adjective returns as the childish ways given up.

In Jam 3:17 the subgroup's word is itself a qualifier: open to reason (G2138, an adjective) is one of a series of qualities said of the wisdom from above, with pure, peaceable, gentle, full of mercy, impartial and sincere, ordered by first and then.
In Act 28:18 a negator reaches the subgroup's word itself: no (G3367) qualifies the cause (G0156), so the verse denies that any ground for the death penalty was found.

In Pro 3:30 the subgroup's word works as a qualifier of the verb: for no reason (H2600, an adverb, without cause) qualifies contend; the negator not (H0408) reaches contend and no (H3808) reaches harm, not the reason.

Where the subgroup's word is a phrase of cause, the negators of the verse reach other words, not the cause: unknown in Gen 41:31 (the plenty), bear, profane and die in Num 18:32, has not come in 1Sa 20:29, the question and know in Mar 12:24, no longer bear in 1Th 3:5.
In Gen 41:31, Gen 47:13 and Eze 19:10 the phrase by reason of governs a noun of cause, and the qualifiers reach that noun: the famine that will follow and is very severe, the abundant water.

In the other verses the qualifiers stand in the clause around the subgroup's word and reach other words: males in Jos 5:4, now in 1Sa 20:29, branches in Eze 19:10, Most High, lives, forever and everlasting of God in Dan 4:34, more greatness in Dan 4:36, vicious crime in Act 18:14, alarmed Felix and the present in Act 24:25, often in Rom 15:22, vain labor in 1Th 3:5, all distress in 1Th 3:7, foremo
In Dan 4:34 the reason is the faculty of a named person: Nebuchadnezzar speaks in the first person, and my reason is his own, the word that returns to him.
In Isa 1:18 the Lord is named as the speaker who calls the people to reason together with him: the reasoning is set between God and the people he addresses.
In Luk 9:47 Jesus is named as the one who knows the reasoning of others: the reasoning belongs to the disciples, referred to by their hearts, and Jesus is the knower of it.

In Act 19:8 and Act 19:9 the one reasoning is referred to by pronoun only (he); the places are named (the synagogue, the hall of Tyrannus) and the disciples are named as those he took with him; God is named in the kingdom of God, the subject of the reasoning. In 1Cor 13:11 the one who reasoned is I, the speaker who became a man.

Where the subgroup's word is a phrase of cause, God is named in the verse, not as the one who reasons: the Lord and God in Job 1:9, Jesus and God in Mar 12:24, Christ Jesus in Eph 3:1 (with I, Paul), Jesus Christ in 1Ti 1:16, God in 2Ti 1:6, Christ the Lord in 1Pe 3:15 (the data gives lord two codes, G2962 and G2316), the Son of God in 1Jo 3:8.

Where the subgroup's word is a phrase of cause, people are named or referred to in the verse: Joshua and the men of war in Jos 5:4, Solomon and David in 1Ki 11:27 (the he who lifted his hand is not named in the verse), Job in Job 1:9, a man in Pro 3:30, the men Peter addresses in Act 10:21, the brothers in 1Th 3:7.

In Act 19:8 and Act 19:9 the reasoning runs outward from one person to others: he reasons with them in the synagogue, about the kingdom of God, and then daily in the hall of Tyrannus, having taken the disciples with him.
In Isa 1:18 the reasoning runs both ways: the Lord speaks and the verb is first person plural, let us, so the reasoning is held together between him and the people.

In Luk 9:47 and 1Cor 13:11 the reasoning is addressed to no one: it is held within, in their hearts, or by the speaker as a child. In Luk 9:47 Jesus' knowing runs toward that inner reasoning from outside it.
In Dan 4:34 the reason moves toward its owner: it returns to Nebuchadnezzar after he lifts his eyes to heaven.

In Act 10:21 and 1Pe 3:15 a reason is an account asked and given: Peter asks the men for the reason of their coming, and the believer gives a reason to anyone who asks; it runs from the one asked to the one asking.
In Job 1:9 and Pro 3:30 the cause is denied: fearing God and contending are said to have no ground behind them.

Where the subgroup's word is a phrase of cause, it points from a ground to an act: to the circumcision in Jos 5:4, the raised hand in 1Ki 11:27, being wrong in Mar 12:24, Paul's sentence in Eph 3:1, which breaks off, being comforted in 1Th 3:7, the mercy received in 1Ti 1:16, the reminder in 2Ti 1:6, the appearing of the Son of God in 1Jo 3:8.
In Dan 4:34 lifted (H5191) stands three words before reason: Nebuchadnezzar lifted his eyes to heaven and his reason returned, two clauses in sequence joined by and; the lifting comes first.
In Act 28:20 asked (G3870) stands two words after the phrase for this reason, which governs it: the cause comes first and the asking to see them follows from it.
In 1Pe 3:15 the reason (G3056) is what is asked for: asks (G0154) stands two words before it, and the one who asks seeks an account of the hope.

In Act 19:9 unbelief (G0544) stands ten words before reasoning: some continued in unbelief, and so he withdrew and took the disciples with him to reason elsewhere; the unbelief of the hearers is what moves the reasoning to the hall of Tyrannus.

In 1Th 3:5, 1Th 3:7 and 1Ti 1:16 the phrase for this reason points ahead to a clause whose object or means is faith: Paul sends to learn of their faith, their faith is the means of the comfort, and the mercy is shown as a pattern for future believers.
In Pro 3:30 harm (H7451C) stands four words after for no reason, in the clause that gives the ground for it: the man has done no harm, so to contend with him is without cause.

In Num 18:32 profane (H2490H) stands in the next sentence, not joined to by reason of it: the reason phrase frees the giver from sin, and the warning not to profane the holy things follows as its own command.
In Dan 4:34 blessed (H1289) stands three words after reason, in the clause that follows its return: once his reason is back, the king blesses the Most High.
In Act 19:8 boldly (G3955) stands directly before reasoning: he spoke boldly, reasoning and persuading them, so the reasoning is part of the bold speaking in the synagogue.
In Act 28:18 liberty (G0630G) stands three words before reason: the wish to release Paul rests on the absence of any cause for a death sentence.

In Jam 3:17 pure (G0053) stands four places before open to reason in one list of the qualities of the wisdom from above: pure comes first, and open to reason follows after then, peaceable and gentle; they are joined only by the list.
In Jos 5:4 war (H4421) stands ten words after reason, in the explanation the reason introduces: the fighting men who left Egypt died on the way, and that is why Joshua circumcised the people.
In 1Th 3:7 comforted (G3870) stands eight words after for this reason, which governs it: the cause comes first and being comforted about them follows from it.

In 1Sa 20:29 commanded (H6680) stands nine words before for this reason, inside the excuse it sums up: the brother's command to be at the sacrifice is part of the cause given for the absence. The data holds a second code at the same place, H1931 (he), joined to the verb.
In Dan 4:34 praised (H7624) stands five words after reason, among the acts of worship that follow its return: blessing, praising and honoring the one who lives forever.
In Jam 3:17 gentle (G1933) stands directly before open to reason, the next quality in the list of the wisdom from above.
In 1Pe 3:15 gentleness (G4240) stands six words after reason and gives the manner of giving it: the defense for the hope is to be made with gentleness and respect.
In 1Pe 3:15 always (G0104) stands seven words before reason and qualifies the readiness to give it: the believer is to be ready at all times with a defense for the hope.
In Dan 4:34 and 1Ti 1:16 the words of lasting time qualify other nouns, not the reason: the everlasting dominion of God, and eternal life at the end of the purpose clause.

In Act 18:4 and Act 19:8 persuade (G3982) stands beside the reasoning (G1256), six and two words after it, joined by and: the reasoning and the persuading are one activity in the synagogue. WordNet relates the subgroup to this collection through argue, a synonym; the verses show the pairing with persuade instead.

In Act 18:14 wrongdoing (G0092) and crime (G4467) stand in the condition before reason: Gallio would have a ground to hear the complaint only if a wrong or a crime were in question; the reason depends on the offence.
In Gen 41:31 and Gen 47:13 severe (H3515) describes the famine that by reason of names as the cause: the severity of the famine is what makes it a cause, of plenty forgotten and of the land wasting.

In 1Sa 20:29 favor (H2580) stands five words before for this reason, inside the request it sums up: David asks leave on the condition of having found favor, and that request is the cause given for his absence.
In Act 24:25 will (G3333, summon) stands seventeen words after reasoned, in Felix's reply: the reasoning ends with Felix sending Paul away and promising to call him later; the words are not joined.
In Act 28:18 wished (G1014) stands four words before reason, and the reason clause gives its ground: the wish to free Paul rests on there being no cause for death.
In 1Jo 3:8 destroy (G3089) stands five words after the reason, in the clause it introduces: the purpose of the appearing of the Son of God is the destroying of the devil's works.
In Num 18:32 die (H4191) closes the warning of the next sentence, eight words after the reason phrase and not joined to it.
In Jos 5:4 died (H4191) stands in the explanation the reason introduces: the death of the generation that came out of Egypt is the cause of the new circumcision.
In Jam 3:17 sincere (G0505) closes the list of the qualities of wisdom that open to reason belongs to, seven places after it; they are joined only by the list.
In Num 18:32 bear (H5375J) opens the verse, two words before by reason of it: the giver will carry no sin, and the reason phrase gives why.
In 1Th 3:5 bear (G4722) stands two words after for this reason, in the clause of the cause: Paul could bear it no longer, and so he sent to learn about their faith.
In 1Ti 1:16 patience (G3115) stands nine words after for this reason, in the purpose it introduces: the mercy was given so that Christ's patience might be shown.
In 1Th 3:5 tempted (G3985G) stands eleven words after for this reason, in the fear that moved the sending: the cause of the sending includes the worry that the tempter had tempted them.
In Mar 12:24 wrong (G4105) stands directly after the reason: the reason is the cause of the error, and the error is named at once.
In Act 19:9 speaking evil (G2551) stands nine words before reasoning: the slander of the Way by some is part of what moved Paul to withdraw and reason elsewhere.
In Gen 47:13 languished (H3856A) stands directly before by reason of: the wasting of the land is the effect, and the famine named after it is the cause.
In Job 1:9 fear (H3372H) stands two words before for no reason: Satan's question asks whether Job's fear of God has no ground behind it; the fear is what the reason is questioned of.

In Act 24:25 alarmed (G1719) stands ten words after reasoned: Felix becomes afraid while Paul reasons about righteousness, self-control and the judgment to come; the alarm follows the content of the reasoning.
In Gen 41:31 plenty (H7647) opens the verse, three words before by reason of: the plenty is what will be forgotten, and the famine named after the reason phrase is why.

In Dan 4:36 was established (H8627) stands fifteen words after reason, at the end of a sequence that begins with its return: reason, then glory, then the counselors' seeking, then the king set again in his kingdom.

In Gen 41:31 follow stands two words after by reason of and describes the famine it governs: the famine that comes after. The data gives the one English word three codes at the same place, H0310A (after), H1931 (it) and H3651C (so).
In 2Ti 1:6 remind (G0363) stands directly after for this reason, which governs it: the cause comes first and the reminder to rekindle the gift follows from it.
In 1Ti 1:16 mercy (G1653) stands two words before for this reason, which gives its purpose: Paul received mercy, and the reason phrase opens why.
In Jam 3:17 mercy (G1656) stands two places after open to reason, the next quality in the list of the wisdom from above.
In Act 17:17 devout persons (G4576) are among those reasoned with: they stand five words after reasoned, joined to the Jews as the hearers in the synagogue.
In 1Pe 3:15 holy (G1161) stands eight words before reason, in the clause that comes first: Christ is set apart as holy in the heart before the readiness to give a reason.
In Luk 9:47 hearts (G2588) stands two words after reasoning and names where the reasoning is: it is the reasoning of their hearts.
In 1Pe 3:15 hearts (G2588) opens the verse, eleven words before reason: the heart is where Christ is honored, and the reason is given outward to the one who asks.
In Dan 4:34 honored (H1922) stands six words after reason, among the acts of worship that follow its return.
In 1Pe 3:15 honor (G0037) and respect (G5401) frame the reason: Christ is honored in the heart before it, and the defense is made with respect after it.
In Act 28:20 hope (G1680) stands nine words after for this reason, in the clause that gives what Paul is bound for: the hope of Israel is why he wears the chain.
In 1Pe 3:15 hope (G1680) is what the reason is given for: it stands two words after reason, which accounts for it.
In Jam 3:17 impartial (G0087) stands six places after open to reason, in the same list of the qualities of the wisdom from above.
In Mar 12:24 know (G6063) stands two words after the reason and gives its content: they are wrong because they do not know the Scriptures nor God's power; the not knowing is the cause.
In Luk 9:47 knowing (G6063) stands directly before reasoning and takes it as its object: Jesus knows the reasoning of their hearts.

In 1Th 3:5 learn (G1097) stands six words after for this reason, in the purpose of the sending: Paul sent to learn about their faith. WordNet relates the subgroup to this collection through conclude, a synonym; the verses show know and learn instead.
In 1Th 3:5 labor (G2873) stands fifteen words after for this reason, in the fear that moved the sending: that their labor among them would come to nothing.
In 1Jo 3:8 works (G2041) is the object of the purpose the reason introduces: the devil's works are what the Son of God appeared to destroy.
In Dan 4:34 lives (H2417) stands seven words after reason and describes God, the one honored once reason returns: he lives forever; it is not joined to the reason.

In Act 24:25 present (G3568) stands thirteen words after reasoned, in Felix's reply: he sends Paul away for now; the reasoning is cut short.
In Act 18:14 open (G0455) stands fifteen words before reason, in the opening clause: Paul was about to speak when Gallio answered; the reason is Gallio's, not Paul's.
In 1Th 3:5 vain (G2756) closes the verse, eighteen words after for this reason, in the fear that moved the sending: that the labor would be empty.
In Job 1:9 answered (H6030B) opens the verse, six words before for no reason: the question whether Job's fear has a cause is Satan's answer to the Lord.

In Pro 3:30 contend (H7378) stands two words before for no reason, which qualifies it: the strife forbidden is strife without cause. WordNet relates the subgroup to this collection through argue, a synonym; the verse pairs the reason with contend instead.
In Jam 3:17 peaceable (G1516) stands two places before open to reason in the list of the qualities of the wisdom from above.
In 1Pe 3:15 prepared (G2092) stands six words before reason: the readiness is to make a defense to the one who asks for the reason; the reason is what the believer is ready to give.
In Act 18:14 accept (G0430) stands directly after reason, which governs it: Gallio would have ground to hear the complaint out, under the condition of a crime; the reason is the ground for accepting.

In Dan 4:34 and Dan 4:36 returned (H8421G) stands directly after reason as its verb: the reason is the subject that comes back to the king; in Dan 4:36 the same verb then brings back his majesty and splendor, for the glory of his kingdom.
In Eze 19:10 abundant (H7227A) stands directly after by reason of and describes the water named as the cause of the vine's fruitfulness. The data gives the word reason here the code H1961 (to be).
In Act 24:25 righteousness (G1343) stands two words after reasoned and is the first subject of the reasoning: Paul reasons about righteousness.
In 1Ti 1:16 perfect (G3956) stands eight words after for this reason and describes the patience shown, not the reason.
In Dan 4:36 sought (H1156) stands thirteen words after reason, in the sequence that follows its return: the king's counselors and lords seek him out again.
In Act 10:21 looking for (G2212) stands two words before reason: the men's seeking of Peter comes first, and Peter then asks the reason for their coming; the reason asked explains the seeking.

In Act 24:25 self-control (G1466) stands four words after reasoned and is the second subject of the reasoning, between righteousness and the judgment to come. The data gives the word a second code at the same place, G2532 (and).
In 1Cor 13:11 gave up (G2673) stands six words after reasoned, in the next sentence: as a man the speaker set aside childish ways, the speaking, thinking and reasoning of the child among them.
In Num 18:32 sin (H2399) stands directly before by reason of it: the giver will carry no sin, and the reason phrase names the contribution as why.

In Isa 1:18 sins (H2399) stands four words after reason, in what the reasoning together concerns: sins red as scarlet made white as snow. The data gives the word a second code at the same place, H1961 (to be).
In 1Jo 3:8 sinning (G0266, G0264) stands nine and three words before the reason: the sinning of the devil from the beginning is what the purpose the reason introduces is aimed against.
In Luk 9:47 took (G1949) stands three words after reasoning: knowing their reasoning, Jesus takes a child; his act answers the reasoning he knows.
In Act 19:9 took (G0873) stands two words before reasoning: Paul takes the disciples apart, and then reasons daily in the hall; the taking aside comes before the new place of reasoning.
In 1Th 3:7 distress (G2347) and affliction (G0318) stand five and seven words after for this reason, in the clause it governs: the comfort came in the midst of their distress and affliction.
In Act 19:9 stubborn (G4645) stands twelve words before reasoning: some hearers harden, and that is the first of the causes that move Paul to withdraw and reason elsewhere.
In Act 24:25 judgment (G2917) stands seven words after reasoned and is the third subject of the reasoning, the judgment to come.

In Jam 3:17 wisdom (G4678) opens the verse as the subject that open to reason describes: open to reason is a quality of the wisdom from above. WordNet relates the subgroup to this collection through understanding and reasonableness, synonyms; the verse joins reason to wisdom as one of its qualities.

may_rest_on_besides.text: In Act 17:2, 17:17, 18:4, 18:19 and 24:25 'reasoned' is Paul's spoken discourse with listeners: in the synagogue and market he argues from the Scriptures and persuades. In Act 24:25 the same word takes topics (righteousness, self-control, judgment) as what he argues about. The sense is speaking to others to convince, not private thinking; the verse names the audience and the place each time.

In 1Cor 13:11 'reasoned' is the child's way of reckoning and weighing things, set beside speaking and thinking as a child; the verse contrasts it with the adult who has put such ways away. It is an inner process (reckoning), not speech to others, unlike the Acts verses.

In Act 19:8 and 19:9 'reasoning' is Paul's discourse in the synagogue for three months and then daily in the hall of Tyrannus, joined to persuading about the kingdom. It is spoken argument with an audience, the same sense as 'reasoned' of the same code in Acts.

In Luk 9:47 'reasoning' is a noun: the inner debate that goes on in the disciples' hearts, which Jesus knows without being told. It is the content of what is reasoned inside, not an act of speaking to anyone; the verse places it in the heart.

In Act 10:21, 28:18, 28:20 and 2Ti 1:6 'reason' is the cause or ground of something: the cause of the men's coming (10:21), the ground for a charge (28:18), and 'for this cause' in 28:20 and 2Ti 1:6. It is a reason that explains why, never a faculty of thinking.

In Rom 15:22 'reason' translates a conjunction of consequence (G1352, therefore): the verse says that this is why Paul has often been hindered from coming. It is a linking word, not a noun of the mind; what it points back to is outside the verse.

In Jam 3:17 'open to reason' is the quality of being ready to be persuaded or yield to others, one of the traits of wisdom from above listed in the verse beside peaceable and gentle. The word is a character trait of the person, not the faculty of reasoning.

In 1Pe 3:15 'a reason' is an account given in answer when someone asks: believers are to be ready to explain the hope that is in them. It is a spoken account to an asker; the honoring of Christ in the heart is set before it in the same verse.

In Jos 5:4 and 1Ki 11:27 'the reason' introduces the explanation of why something was done: why Joshua circumcised the men, and why he lifted his hand against the king, the one who did it being named only in the verse before. The Hebrew word means a matter or account, here the matter that accounts for the deed.

In Eze 19:10 'by reason of' marks the cause of the vine's fruitfulness: abundant water. The English phrase renders a Hebrew verb of becoming and the sense is simply 'because of'; no mind or thinking is in view.

In Job 1:9 and Pro 3:30 'for no reason' is 'without cause': Satan asks whether Job fears God without gain, and the proverb forbids quarrel with a person who has done no harm. The Hebrew word means gratuitously, with nothing to account for the act.

In Isa 1:18 'let us reason together' is an invitation from the Lord to argue the case out, to set the matter right between the parties, as in a court. It is spoken argument with another, and the verse ties it to the cleansing that follows.

In 1Sa 20:29 'for this reason' is the speaker's report of why the one absent has not come to the king's table: the clan's sacrifice and his brother's command. The word is a linking 'therefore' pointing back to those grounds, not a noun; the speaker and the absent one are named in the verse before.

In Dan 4:34 and 4:36 'my reason' is Nebuchadnezzar's understanding, the sound mind that returns to him when he lifts his eyes to heaven. It names the faculty of mind itself, not a cause; its loss is told before these verses.
In Gen 41:31 and 47:13 'by reason of' is 'because of' with the famine as the cause: the plenty will be unknown and the land languishes. It is a preposition of cause; no mind or thinking is in view.

older_inner_being.text: 4. God's rule (Dan 4:17): *"to the end that the living may know that the Most High rules the kingdom of men and gives it to whom he will and sets over it the lowliest of men."* The passage: the same sentence again (4:25); the king's boast, *"Is not this great Babylon, which I have built by my mighty power … for the glory of my majesty?"* (4:30); the end: *"my reason returned to me, and I blessed the Most High … for his dominion is an everlasting dominion"* (4:34); *"those who walk in pride he is able to humble"* (4:37)

The return: *"my reason returned to me, and I blessed the Most High"* (4:34), and *"he does according to his will among the host of heaven and among the inhabitants of the earth; and none can stay his hand"* (4:35); *"those who walk in pride he is able to humble"* (4:37).

2.2 Passages where Scripture itself puts them together: Pro 1:29–31. Did not choose the fear of the Lord, would have none of my counsel, are filled with their own devices: choosing, willing and devising in one sentence. Earlier in the same chapter, *"if sinners entice you, do not consent. If they say, 'Come with us, let us lie in wait for blood'"* (1:10–11) puts the will's "no" right against a group plot. That is plotting as written in 10.10.; Psa 81:11–12. Would not submit, given over to stubborn hearts, to follow their own counsels.; Isa 30:1, 9, 15–16. A plan *"but not mine"*; unwilling to hear; unwilling, and *"No! We will flee upon horses."* The refusal and the people's own plan are in their own mouth together.; 1Ch 28:19–21. The plan from the hand of the Lord, and *"every willing man who has skill"*. This is the positive pairing: a plan given, and the willing who carry it out.; Gen 24:5–8. Planning ahead allows for another person's will (*"Perhaps the woman may not be willing"*).; 2Sa 13:24–28. A planner presses another's will until it gives way, and the plan goes on to murder.; Mat 1:19–20. Unwilling, then resolved, while still considering, then redirected by God.; Act 12:3–5. Herod's intending is set beside the church's prayer.; 2Co 1:15–17. Wanting, then plans, then the question of a divided word.; Act 27:42–43. One man's wish against a group's plan.; Dan 4:27–35. Counsel offered and not taken; the human will made absolute; the Most High *"does according to his will"*; reason returned.
The heart is where thoughts come from

The thoughts of people are open to God and to Jesus: God discerns, knows and understands them (Ps 139:2; 1Chr 28:9; Isa 66:18), Jesus perceives them (Luke 5:22; Matt 9:4), and the word of God discerns them (Heb 4:12); the speaker of Ps 139:23 asks God to know his thoughts.
Inner reasoning becomes outward quarrel when it is shared and set on one's own standing

1.10 Heart and mind (nous / dianoia) side by side: "put my laws into their minds, and write them on their hearts" / "on their hearts … on their minds" (Heb 8:10 / 10:16); "guard your hearts and your minds" (Phili 4:7); The love command lists heart, soul, mind and strength as separate items (Mar 12:30; Mat 22:37; Luk 10:27); Revisit 2026-09-28 (context Mar 12:28–34, Batch F §2): the scribe repeats the command as "heart … understanding [*synesis*] … strength" (12:33). He replaces soul with a knowing word, and Jesus calls the answer wise (12:34). The faculty list is not fixed; what stays constant is "all".; "evil thoughts [reasonings]" come "out of the heart" (Mat 15:19; Mar 7:21); "the reasoning of their hearts" (Luk 9:47)

d. Thinking, planning, understanding, remembering: *Plans and devising:* Pro 16:1, 9; 19:21; 6:14, 18; 24:2; 12:20; Psa 140:2; 58:2; Zec 7:10; 8:17; Isa 10:7; Act 5:4; Eze 38:10.; *Understanding and knowing:*; "a heart to understand" (Deu 29:4); "understanding mind" (1Ki 3:9); "understand with their hearts" (Isa 6:10; Mat 13:15; Joh 12:40; Act 28:27); "an intelligent heart acquires knowledge" (Pro 18:15); "the heart of the hasty will understand" (Isa 32:4); *Remembering and "laying to heart":*; Isa 47:7; 57:1, 11; 42:25; Mal 2:2; Jer 12:11; Ecc 7:2; 9:1; Deu 4:39; 32:46; 1Sa 21:12; "call to mind" (Lam 3:21; Deu 30:1); "come into mind" (Jer 3:16; 7:31; 19:5; 32:35; 44:21; 51:50; Isa 65:17); Haggai's repeated "Consider your ways" is literally *set your heart* (Hag 1:5, 7; 2:15, 18) [lexical].; *Searching and investigating:* "I applied my heart to seek and to search out" (Ecc 1:13, 17; 7:25; 8:9, 16); "great searchings of heart" (Judg 5:15–16).; *Pondering and treasuring:* Mary "treasured up all these things, pondering them in her heart" (Luk 2:19, 51); "ponder in your own hearts on your beds" (Psa 4:4); "the meditation of my heart" (Psa 19:14; 49:3).; *Questioning and reasoning:* Mar 2:6, 8; Luk 3:15; 5:22; 9:47; 24:38.
Luk 9:45–47: perception blocked from outside → fear to ask → rivalry → Jesus knows the reasoning of their hearts (v3)

1. The heart or mind is the place thoughts come from. Mark 7:21 and Matt 15:19 ("out of the heart come evil thoughts"). Also: "a heart that devises wicked plans" (Prov 6:18); "plan evil things in their heart" (Ps 140:2); "devise evil … in your heart" (Zech 7:10; 8:17); "The heart of man plans his way" (Prov 16:9); "his heart does not so think; but it is in his heart to destroy" (Isa 10:7); "the reasoning of their hearts" (Luke 9:47); In Jer 4:14, thoughts *lodge* within: "How long shall your wicked thoughts lodge within you?" This follows the call to "wash your heart."

*dialogizomai / dialogismos* | Honest troubled reasoning · hardened anxious reasoning · inner questioning seen by Jesus · reasoning together into murder · self-talk of the rich man · quarrel, dispute, opinions · argument about greatness · futile thinking · evil thoughts from the heart · partiality: "judges with evil thoughts" · thoughts revealed by the child set for a sign | Luk 1:29 · Mar 8:16–17; Mat 16:7–8 · Mar 2:6, 8; Luk 5:21–22; 6:8; 9:47 · Luk 20:14; Mat 21:25 · Luk 12:17 · 1Ti 2:8 ("without anger or quarreling"); Phili 2:14; Rom 14:1 · Luk 9:46 · Rom 1:21; 1Co 3:20 · Mar 7:21; Mat 15:19 · Jam 2:4 · Luk 2:35 | Inner reasoning becomes outward quarrel when it is shared and set on one's own standing (Luk 9:46; Rom 14:1) (R). The heart state decides honest or hardened (Luk 1:29 against Mar 8:17, S). In 1Ti 2:8 the quarrel word stands beside anger, a link to the anger strand

What the angry person does with it: Nehemiah: "I took counsel with myself"; Absalom "spoke to Amnon neither good nor bad"; Jacob's sons answered "deceitfully"; Samuel "cried to the Lord all night"; David "was afraid of the Lord that day"; Sanballat and Tobiah "plotted together"; Ahab "lay down on his bed and turned away his face"; Paul "reasoned in the synagogue".
A person's anger leads to counsel, then open charge; reasoning: "I took counsel with myself, and I brought charges against the nobles"; "So he reasoned in the synagogue".
his spirit provoked as he saw idols → so he reasoned (Act 17:16–17); many days → greatly annoyed → commanded the spirit → it came out (16:18).

Part 2 verses: what they add. The one wronged is now God, or God's law, rather than a sister, a friend or the poor: The indignation seizes its bearer: "Hot indignation seizes me because of the wicked, who forsake your law" (Psa 119:53). The bearer is its object as well as its subject. It is framed between comfort in God's rules (119:52) and "Your statutes have been my songs" (119:54). The indignation sits inside a life held by the law it defends; The spirit provoked by what it sees: "while Paul was waiting … his spirit was provoked within him as he saw that the city was full of idols. So he reasoned in the synagogue … and in the marketplace every day" (Act 17:16–17). This is the same movement as Neh 5:6–7: indignation, then an inner act, then public speech. Here the seat is named in the indignation verse itself; Annoyance that finally acts: the slave girl "kept doing this for many days. Paul, having become greatly annoyed, turned and said to the spirit, 'I command you … come out of her'" (Act 16:18); What annoys him is a true proclamation ("These men are servants of the Most High God", 16:17) from a wrong source; The anger builds over "many days" before the act; The act sets off anger in others: "when her owners saw that their hope of gain was gone, they seized Paul and Silas" (16:19).
Thinking matures ("I thought like a child … I gave up childish ways")

6.4 Hope and the NT inner seat: "my heart was glad … my flesh also will dwell in hope" (Act 2:26) — flesh in hope; "hope does not put us to shame, because God's love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit" (Rom 5:5) [D1]; "by the power of the Holy Spirit you may abound in hope" (Rom 15:13) [D1]; "through the Spirit, by faith, we ourselves eagerly wait for the hope of righteousness" (Gal 5:5) [D3]; "one body and one Spirit … one hope" (Eph 4:4) [D1]; "the eyes of your hearts enlightened, that you may know what is the hope" (Eph 1:18); "in your hearts honor Christ … a reason for the hope that is in you" (1Pe 3:15); "waiting for the consolation of Israel, and the Holy Spirit was upon him" (Luk 2:25) [D1]

earlier_readings.text: Reasoning is a done act of speech in seven Acts verses: Paul reasons in the synagogue, in the marketplace, in the hall of Tyrannus and before Felix (Act 17:2, 17:17, 18:4, 18:19, 19:8, 19:9, 24:25). The verb stands in the aorist or imperfect and is spoken to hearers, with persuading beside it in several; it is an exchange of grounds in speech and not a silent act.

In Luk 9:47 the reasoning is inward: it is in the hearts of the disciples after their dispute, and it is Jesus who knows it, the knowing standing 1 word before the member. The same noun therefore gives an unspoken reasoning here and the spoken reasoning of the Acts verses.
In 1Cor 13:11 the reckoning is the working out of a child and is set among speaking and thinking as one of the ways of a child; the verb is a past tense and is given up when the speaker became a man.

What the reasoning is on, where the verses give it, is the Scriptures in Act 17:2, the topics of righteousness, self-control and judgment before Felix in Act 24:25 and the kingdom of God in Act 19:8; the objects are matters of teaching put to hearers, with persuading as the aim in Act 18:4, 19:8.

In the ground phrases 'for this reason' and 'the reason why' (G1223, G5124, G5484, G1352, G0156) the member names the ground on which an act or state stands: Paul's sending to learn of faith (1Th 3:5), the comfort he received (1Th 3:7), the mercy received (1Ti 1:16), his imprisonment and prayer (Eph 3:1, Eph 3:14), his hindering (Rom 15:22), the chain he wears (Act 28:20) and the reminder to Timothy (2Ti 1:6). In each the ground is stated first and what rests on it follows, 8 to 13 words later where the stored positions are given.

The ground is set beside bearing and sin in four verses: sin is not borne by reason of the offering (Num 18:32), Paul could bear it no longer and sent (1Th 3:5), the sins are what the reasoning together addresses (Isa 1:18), and the Son of God appeared on the ground of the devil's sinning (1Jo 3:8). The reasoning or the ground is thus named where a burden or a sin stands within a few words.

Knowing is stated as the ground of error in Mar 12:24: the ground of the error is a lack of knowledge, of the Scriptures and of God's power, and the negator reaches the knowing. In Luk 9:47 the knowing is Jesus' knowing of the disciples' reasoning. The ground and the knowing stand within two words of each other in both verses.

The ground is denied in four verses: 'for no reason' (Job 1:9, Pro 3:30), no reason for the death penalty (Act 28:18) and the question whether this is not the reason (Mar 12:24). The negator reaches the reason itself in the first three, so the ground is stated as absent; in Mar 12:24 the question puts it as the answer.

Where the ground is denied (Job 1:9, Pro 3:30, Act 28:18) the act is a refusal of a ground: Satan asks whether Job fears God for nothing, the proverb forbids contending without cause, and the Romans found no ground for the penalty.

Two qualifiers give the reasoning its manner and length: 'three' Sabbath days in Act 17:2 (2 words before) gives how long it went on, and 'like a child' in 1Cor 13:11 (1 before and 2 after) gives the kind of reckoning. The qualifier of the ground in Rom 15:22 is 'often', which gives the repeated hindering the reason accounts for.

Reasoning and the ground run in different directions across the verses: from Paul to hearers in the Acts verses, from Jesus to those he answers in Mar 12:24, from the Lord to the people in Isa 1:18, and from God to Paul in 1Ti 1:16, where mercy is received for this reason. God and Jesus are named more often than any human in these verses, and Paul, who reasons in the Acts verses, is not among the stored entities.

Believing meets the reasoning in four verses. In Act 19:9 the unbelief is 10 words before Paul's reasoning, as what the reasoning meets; in 1Th 3:5, 1Th 3:7 and 1Ti 1:16 faith or believing is 8 to 13 words after the phrase 'for this reason', as what the ground leads to. The reasoning answers unbelief, and the stated ground is followed by faith.

Words of duration stand 7 to 17 words from the reasoning or the ground in three verses (Dan 4:34, 1Ti 1:16, 1Pe 3:15), in other clauses and phrases (the everlasting kingdom, eternal life, always being prepared). The two meet only in that the verse says something is lasting beside the ground; no tie of grammar joins them.

Bearing meets the ground in three verses: 'bear' is 2 words before the ground in Num 18:32 (bear no sin by reason of it) and 2 after in 1Th 3:5 (could bear it no longer), and 'patience' is 9 after in 1Ti 1:16. The ground is stated in the same clause as the bearing in the first two.

Knowing meets the reasoning and the ground in three verses. In Mar 12:24 the ground of the error is the lack of knowing (2 words after the phrase of reason) and the negator reaches the knowing; in Luk 9:47 Jesus' knowing is 1 word before the reasoning in the disciples' hearts; in 1Th 3:5 learning is 6 after the ground. Knowing is the ground or the knower of the reasoning.

Sin meets the ground and the reasoning in three verses: sin is 1 word before the reason in Num 18:32 (no sin borne by reason of the offering), 4 after the reasoning together in Isa 1:18, and 3 and 9 before the ground in 1Jo 3:8 (the devil sinning from the beginning). Sin is the matter the reasoning addresses or the ground that is stated.
